extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students interested in the history and foundations of number theory
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-textbook style exposition tracing number-lore: figurate numbers, divisibility properties, primes, perfect and amicable numbers, primality tests, Fermat's problems, and foundational issues (infinity, axioms, nature of proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurate (triangular and square) numbers and their relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangular numbers (1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ...) and square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25) were represented by dots; the Pythagoreans knew that a square number of rank n equals the triangular number of the same rank increased by its predecessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained geometrically by segregating dots; algebraically triangular number of rank n = 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2 and predecessor gives n^2 when added. The text emphasizes the historical importance of geometrical intuition as a proof method and compares it to modern algebraic derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurate-number representation as proof method
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Greek proofs used dot-arrangements (figurative representations) to demonstrate number relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Pythagoreans 'proved it by segregating the dots and counting them' — an experimental/concrete visual proof method contrasting later abstract algebraic proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of amicable numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Two numbers are amicable if the sum of the proper divisors of each equals the other (example: divisors of 284 sum to 220, divisors of 220 sum to 284).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Greeks found such couples difficult and of interest; the text notes historical appearances (Hindus, Biblical references) and cultural anecdotes (gematria story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: excessive, defective, and perfect numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: A number is excessive if it is greater than the sum of its proper divisors, defective if less, and perfect if it equals the sum of its proper divisors (examples: 6 and 28 are perfect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives examples and cultural significance (biblical commentators, St. Augustine). It notes empirical observations (even perfect numbers end in 6 or 8) and historical enumeration by Nicomachus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid's construction of even perfect numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's theorem: any number of the form 2^{n-1}(2^n - 1) is perfect if the second factor (2^n - 1) is prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By taking n = 1, 2, 4, 6, ... one obtains known perfect numbers; Euler later proved that every even perfect number is of this form. The text remarks on experimental difficulty (large perfect numbers have many digits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes for primes
rubrics_metrics.description: List integers in order and eliminate multiples successively (first multiples of 2, then remaining multiples of 3, then 5, etc.) to obtain primes up to a bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributed to Eratosthenes; practical limits: to find primes < 1000 need only cross out multiples up to 31 because 31^2 < 1000. The sieve is inductive and effective for table construction but not for proving general properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid's factorial-based proof of infinitely many primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid shows that for any finite list of primes (or using n!), the number n! + 1 either is prime or has prime divisors greater than n, proving there is no greatest prime (primes are infinite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces factorials (n!) and Euclid numbers (n! + 1). The argument uses that consecutive numbers have no common divisors; examples illustrate both possibilities (n=3 gives prime, n=7 gives composite 5041 = 71^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorials (n!) as a tool / notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorial n! is the product of the first n positive integers (used in Euclid's argument and subsequent tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A table of factorials up to 11! is referenced. The text treats factorials as important objects in number-theoretic constructions and primality arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple divisibility heuristics (end-digit and rule of nine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick tests: a number is composite if it ends in 5, 0, or an even digit; for 3 and 9 use the 'rule of nine' — if the sum of digits is a multiple of 3 or 9, the number is divisible by 3 or 9 respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as old and practically useful rules; the text notes that for larger divisors conditions are more involved and general theorems (Pascal, Lagrange) have limited practical value for very large numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat numbers and danger of incomplete induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Fermat proposed numbers F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1 (first few: 3, 5, 17, 257, 65537) and believed they were all prime; Euler later showed F_5 is composite, illustrating the danger of extrapolating from finitely many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a cautionary historical lesson: many quadratic expressions can generate primes for many initial n but fail later (example given where expression is prime for n=1..40 but composite at n=41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat's little theorem as necessary-only primality test
rubrics_metrics.description: Fermat's theorem: for prime p and integer a, a^p ≡ a (mod p); the condition is necessary but not sufficient (composites like 341 can satisfy the congruence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is useful as an indirect test, but pseudoprimes (Carmichael/Fermat liars) show it is not a definitive criterion by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wilson's theorem as a necessary and sufficient primality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilson's theorem: p is prime iff (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) — equivalently, (p − 1)! + 1 is divisible by p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes its theoretical importance but emphasizes computational impracticality: verifying (p − 1)! + 1 for large p is as hard as direct primality testing. A 'Wilson number' (remainder) table is discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goldbach's conjecture (status and empirical verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture: every even number is the sum of two primes; historically verified by computation up to large bounds (text cites verification up to 200,000,000) but remains unproved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a central unsolved problem that has withstood major efforts; the text frames it among other major conjectures motivating research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution/density of primes and twin-primes remark
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about how primes are distributed: density (number of primes below x) and conjectures/partial results (Bertrand's postulate, Chebyshev, Bonolis' approximation). Twin primes become rarer — Brun proved results about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bertrand asserted a prime between n and 2n (proved by later work); Bonolis gave an approximate formula for primes between x and 2x; Brun (1919) proved twin primes thin out (Brun's theorem). The text contrasts precise results with remaining open distribution questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean triples and parametrization
rubrics_metrics.description: Integer solutions to x^2 + y^2 = z^2 are infinite; Diophantus gave rules; formulae in modern notation express all Pythagorean triplets (parametrized by integers u, v with certain conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides the parametric formulas (involving u and v) and emphasizes the infinite family and derivability of all such integer right-triangles from the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat's Last Theorem: statement, partial results, and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fermat's claim: x^n + y^n = z^n has no nontrivial integer solutions for n > 2. Historical partial proofs exist for many exponents; the general case resisted proof and stimulated major advances (e.g., Kummer's ideal numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recounts historical progress (Euler, Dirichlet, Kummer) and notes the problem spawned substantial new mathematics; also comments on the many incorrect claimed proofs and a prize that stimulated amateur attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational properties of arithmetic operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition and multiplication satisfy commutativity and associativity; multiplication distributes over addition. These properties form the elementary axioms underlying arithmetic procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains these properties in pedagogical terms with examples (e.g., adding 25 + 34 by decomposing into tens and units) and argues their foundational role in education and subsequent mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual problem of 'all numbers' and infinity as an axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim 'all numbers' leads to the problem of infinity: there is no last number and therefore one cannot verify properties by exhaustion; the inexhaustibility of counting is a basic mathematical assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses philosophical/historical perspectives (experience vs. assumption), Archimedes' Sand Reckoner as illustration of large finite numbers, and ancient views that 'the last number belonged to the gods.' This motivates formal methods (induction, axiomatization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic method and desiderata for axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: In setting up axioms one desires premises that are free from contradiction, independent, and exhaustive (completely cover the question under investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text locates axiomatics in the work of Peano, Russell, Hilbert, and explains its role in transforming logic into mathematical practice; it frames foundational disputes (intuitionists vs. formalists) about the nature of proof and mathematical existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive vs. experimental/inductive methods in number theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Number theory historically had an 'experimental' character: conjectures arrived from mass computations and later (often much later) received rigorous proofs; deductive reasoning starts from axioms/definitions and derives consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations (G. H. Hardy) emphasize conjecture-from-computation pattern; the text contrasts the concreteness of early number lore with later abstract deductive approaches and raises philosophical questions about what constitutes proof.
